AI for All is X-lab AI's long-term goal and a public invitation to act. We want more people to afford AI and develop the capability to use it well. Those are connected ambitions: access gives people an opportunity to begin, while learning and practical work help turn that opportunity into useful results. We begin with developer communities, broadly understood to include learners, builders and engineers. The framework in this presentation explains how open technology, human creativity, public goods and sustained support can work together.

Linux provides a historical reference for open collaboration. Its thirty-five-year journey shows how a project can become shared infrastructure through contributions, maintenance and adoption. The lesson is broader than making something available at no charge. Value depends on people continuing to improve, maintain and use it. We draw on that experience as we think about AI, while recognizing that AI brings its own technical and social challenges. The Linux anniversary material is an illustration of open collaboration, not an endorsement of this manifesto.

Open AI models give more developers opportunities to learn, build and adapt. These examples are Alibaba's Qwen, DeepSeek, Zhipu AI's GLM, Moonshot AI's Kimi and Tencent's Hunyuan. The releases shown are examples, not a current ranking or an exhaustive list. Licenses differ across releases and should be checked for each use. What matters to our narrative is the connection between access to model capabilities, developers' applications and improvements, and real settings where people can benefit.

Two forces reinforce each other. Open source lowers barriers by making technology, knowledge and tools available for learning, improvement and reuse. Developers bring judgment and creativity, turning those resources into useful applications. Developers include people exploring AI for the first time, building applications, or engineering systems for sustained use. Our multiplication formula expresses this mutual reinforcement. It is a conceptual statement, not a numerical formula for measuring social impact. Outcomes still need to be tested in practice.

Our path connects AI to inclusion through digital public goods. Developers can turn capabilities into reusable software, data and knowledge. Sharing is an important step, but real benefit also depends on documentation, maintenance, adoption and local adaptation. We need to understand the people who use a result, the conditions in which they use it, and the problems they still face. Digital public goods are an intended path; a particular solution's compliance with any formal standard requires evidence.

Data and evaluation form the shared core. Platforms connect people and practice. Data make evidence traceable. Evaluation methods help interpret contributions and outcomes. Research examines the methods themselves. These kinds of work interact rather than forming a fixed sequence. The aim is to make contributions visible, match resources with needs and examine whether action helps. Evaluation should support growth, with transparent limitations and channels for correction. A single score cannot define a person's worth.

The growth cycle begins with contribution and practice. Recognition and learning help people build capability, improving public goods and applications. The resource cycle connects support with useful results and evidence for continued investment. The two cycles reinforce each other: public goods create value, while resources support people and sustained practice. Data and evaluation connect both cycles. Practice supplies evidence; evaluation informs the next decisions. These are relationships we intend to test and improve, not a promise of automatic growth or guaranteed returns.

We can build on practical foundations. OpenDigger provides open-source data and metrics. OpenRank offers methods for understanding contributions through collaboration networks. OpenShare explores connections among contributions, capabilities, organizational needs and resources. These existing projects provide ways to begin. They should not be presented as evidence that this initiative has already achieved its inclusion goals. Our current action is the public co-creation of the manifesto and its materials, with progress and limitations recorded openly.

Participation can start with a real need. Developers can share feedback and contribute tools, documentation or cases. Communities can organize learning and collaboration, bringing back experience from adoption. Partners can offer resources and practical settings for work that can be evaluated. Basic participation does not require an existing contribution score. Resource conditions belong in each action's public description. The launch page brings the manifesto, materials and participation routes together, so audiences can choose a concrete next step.

This is the complete framework: one goal, two forces, one shared core, two reinforcing cycles and three complementary perspectives on inclusion. Digital public goods connect creation to real help through adoption and local adaptation. Developers, the public and the Global South are complementary perspectives, not mutually exclusive groups or sequential stages. We invite people to begin with a need, a contribution or a practical setting. Visit the launch page, read the manifesto and help us turn a shared direction into accountable action.
